headline: Australia banned teen social media. Did it work?

sources.title: Most Australian teens still online three months after under-16 ban (Al Jazeera)
Australia's under-16 social media ban failing, study shows (Al Jazeera)
Why young people say the social media ban is not working (ABC News Australia)
Australia's social media ban is failing, new study suggests (video, CBS Boston)

chunks.text: In December 2025, Australia became the first country in the world to [[ban]] [[social media]] for everyone under 16. The law was [[designed]] to {{keep out}} young teenagers, closing the doors of TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat to young users. [[Platforms]] {{shut down}} about 4.7 million [[accounts]], and parents hoped their children would spend less time on [[screens]]. New [[data]] tells a different story: most under-16s are still online, and many use the apps just as often as before.

verbs.why: Fences keep out wild animals, and passwords keep out strangers. The law was written to keep young teenagers out of the biggest apps.

verbs.wrong: To sell to a bigger company
verbs.why: Factories shut down in a crisis, and websites shut down for repairs. The platforms shut down about 4.7 million underage accounts.

chunks.text: How do teenagers stay online? The country's [[internet regulator]] found that about half of the children who kept their accounts were never even asked to [[prove]] their age. Others simply {{signed up}} again with a false [[date of birth]], or used [[tricks]] to {{get around}} the [[age checks]]. Some fooled [[face scans]] with photos of older people. One teenager said a friend passed the scan using a printed photo of a famous singer. Still others {{switched over}} to smaller apps that the law does not cover.

verbs.correct: To join a service with your details
verbs.wrong: To pay a monthly service fee
verbs.why: People sign up for gym memberships, newsletters, and free trials. Many teens just signed up again with a false date of birth.

verbs.correct: To avoid a rule in a clever way
verbs.wrong: To read a rule very carefully
verbs.why: Drivers get around tolls by taking back roads, and kids get around bedtime rules by pretending to be asleep. Teens found many ways to get around the age checks.

verbs.correct: To change to a different service
verbs.wrong: To pay for a premium version
verbs.why: Families switch over to cheaper phone plans, and viewers switch over to another channel. Some teens switched over to apps the law does not cover.

chunks.text: The numbers are [[hard to argue with]]. Before the ban, 86 percent of Australian children under 16 used social media. Three months after it began, the [[figure]] was 81 percent, and daily use had [[barely]] moved, from about 60 percent to 58 percent. Many teenagers who left at first have {{come back}}, and news reports in August 2026 said most under-16s use the apps just as often as before the ban. Only a small number have truly {{given up}} their accounts. Kids who {{slip through}} the checks [[rarely]] get caught, because the platforms hardly ever {{follow up}}.

verbs.why: Customers come back to a store they like, and birds come back every spring. Many teens who left the apps in December have quietly come back.
People give up sugar, old habits, and gym memberships. Only a small number of teens have truly given up their accounts.

verbs.correct: To pass a check without being caught
verbs.wrong: To report a problem to a website
verbs.why: Small mistakes can slip through an inspection, and a broken part can slip through the final test at a factory. Kids who slip through the age checks rarely get caught, because platforms check very little.

verbs.correct: To check again after a first action
verbs.why: Doctors follow up with patients after surgery, and sellers follow up on unpaid bills. Kids who slip through the age checks rarely get caught, because the platforms hardly ever follow up.

chunks.text: The government is not ready to {{back down}}. [[Ministers]] point to the millions of closed accounts and say the law has changed how families talk about phones. [[Officials]] compare it to [[age limits]] on alcohol: nobody expects perfect [[compliance]], but the rule still matters. The regulator wants platforms to {{crack down}} with stronger age checks, and companies that fail to act may face heavy [[fines]]. Meanwhile, in living rooms across Australia, teenagers quietly {{log on}}, and the world watches an [[experiment]] that many other countries want to copy.

verbs.correct: To change your mind under pressure
verbs.wrong: To announce a bigger new plan
verbs.why: A boss can back down after workers protest, and a country can back down in a trade fight. Australia's government refuses to back down on the ban.

verbs.correct: To get tough on rule breaking
verbs.wrong: To ask users for their opinions
verbs.why: Police crack down on speeding, and schools crack down on cheating. The regulator wants platforms to crack down with stronger age checks.
Workers log on every morning, and students log on for online classes. Across Australia, teenagers quietly log on despite the ban.

mainIdea.s: Months after the world's first under-16 social media ban, most young Australians are still online and use the apps as often as before. The government wants stronger age checks.
mainIdea.why: About 81 percent of under-16s still use social media, and ministers compare the law to age limits on alcohol.

mainIdea.s: Most young Australians deleted their accounts for good once the pioneering law against teen apps took effect. The government plans to end the ban because it is no longer needed.
mainIdea.why: Close, but most under-16s never really left, and the government refuses to back down rather than ending the law.

mainIdea.s: Australia's highest court has canceled the country's social media rules for children under sixteen. Judges ruled the law unfair because adults never had to prove their age.
mainIdea.why: No court canceled anything. The ban still stands, and the debate is about weak age checks, not a ruling.

tf.s: Australia was the first country to ban social media for under-16s.
tf.why: The law took effect in December 2025 and was designed to keep young teens out of the big apps.

tf.s: Platforms shut down about 4.7 million accounts.
tf.why: Even so, most under-16s stayed online or came back later.

tf.s: Every child who kept an account had to pass a strict age check.
tf.why: About half were never asked to prove their age at all, the regulator found, so many accounts slipped through without a check.

tf.s: Some teens fooled face scans with photos of older people.
tf.why: Some got around the face scans with photos of older people, and one even passed using a printed photo of a famous singer.

tf.s: The government has decided to back down and end the ban.
tf.why: Ministers defend the law and want platforms to crack down with stronger age checks.

tf.s: Daily social media use among under-16s fell sharply after the ban.
tf.why: Daily use barely moved, from about 60 percent before the ban to 58 percent three months after it began.
